newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian rebels say talks only way to end siege.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian rebels say talks only way to end siege.

text.p: Entrenched Marxist guerrillas holding 74 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Peru told President Alberto Fujimori on Saturday there could be no end to the crisis without negotiations.
"Nobody in here is giving up," was their defiant message that greeted Peru at dawn on the 18th day of the standoff.

Under cover of darkness, rebels of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) crawled across the roof of the besieged diplomatic mansion and unfurled three banners in reply to Fujimori's uncompromising speech two days ago.
"Mr Fujimori, with arrogant declarations and without dialogue, there will never be a solution," one banner said.
The other two said:
"Mothers, wives and children of our prisoners are also waiting for their freedom. Peace for all Peruvians."
"Today's Peru -- 13 million Peruvians in extreme poverty. Where is the progress?"
The guerrillas also hoisted their red flag, emblazoned with a mace and rifle and the image of Tupac Amaru -- an 18th-century Andean Indian who led a bloody uprising against Spanish colonial rule.

The 20-odd, heavily armed guerrillas stormed the residence on Dec. 17 during a reception in honour of Japanese Emperor Akihito and are demanding the release of some 400 MRTA members from Peruvian prisons.
Fujimori on Thursday rejected the rebels' claim to be fighting poverty in Peru and condemned them as "terrorists" bent on violence. He has ruled out freeing any MRTA prisoners.
But with the two sides giving no ground, there were fresh concerns over a possibile violent solution to the standoff.
In Tokyo, Foreign Ministry spokesman Hiroshi Hashimoto said the prospects of winning the release of the high-level hostages were now worse than at any time since the seizure of the residence.
"The situation is more serious than ever before. Dialogue began before the new year between the MRTA and the Peruvian government but now it has reached an impasse," he said.
Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said the release of 450 hostages since the siege began meant the jungle-trained guerrillas now had greater control over remaining captives.
"I am not optimistic about the situation, seeing as the number of hostages has been reduced to a level where it is easy for the terrorists to control them," he told reporters.

Tokyo also snuffed out speculation a deal could be cut to release some hostages. "I would like to make it plain once again that neither Peru nor Japan have any intention of paying a ransom," Hiroshi Hashimoto said.

The only activity at the siege site on Saturday was the usual ferrying of food and cleaning materials by Red Cross workers, who have gradually improved the hostages' comfort inside the cramped residence.

Peru's negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, stayed away from the site. Nor was there any sign of Red Cross mediator Michel Minnig or talks' observer Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, who have both regularly visited the compound.

Following last week's first face-to-face meeting between Palermo and the guerrillas, Fujimori has kept his negotiator out of the building despite MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa's assurance that "the doors are open."
Frustration at the entrenched position of both sides has led to calls for various personalities to enter negiotiations as mediators.
Guatemala's ambassador to Peru and former hostage, Jose Maria Argueta, has offered to return to captivity to help.
Peru's ombudsman, Jorge Santistevan -- requested by the MRTA as mediator at the start of the siege -- threw his hat into the ring on Friday.
Opposition legislator Harold Forsyth said former U.S. president Jimmy Carter should be invited to broker a deal.
Fujimori has ignored all such proposals.

Throughout the crisis he has refused all military or diplomatic aid from foreign governments. The ambassador's residence is technically Japanese territory, but despite starting the siege with sharp differences, Tokyo has ceded all control to the Peruvian president.
The rebels have not freed any hostages since Wednesday when seven were released following a visit by Cipriani -- a close friend of Fujimori.
The remaining captives included Fujimori's brother, two ambassadors, top Peruvian government officials and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
